## 2 Kings 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

The chapter falls into three sections: (1) the Shunammite woman's land restored (vv. 1–6); (2) Elisha in Damascus — Hazael's rise (vv. 7–15); (3) the wicked reigns of Jehoram and Ahaziah in Judah (vv. 16–29).

---

### v. 1 — *"Now Elisha had said to the woman whose son he had restored to life…"*

- The Hebrew has no "then"; the better rendering is "Now Elisha had spoken," indicating a flashback to a time long before the siege of Samaria. The famine is probably the one mentioned in 2 Kings 4:38. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Elisha grounds his command in a relationship already marked by grace: the Shunammite woman had experienced God's power in the miraculous birth and resurrection of her son. "Past grace becomes the foundation for present obedience." The threefold command — arise, go, sojourn — emphasizes urgency. She is not told a specific destination, only to "sojourn wherever you can"; her safety lies in obedience, not geography. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-8-commentary)
- "The LORD has called for a famine" — the phrase reveals God's sovereign control over natural and national events. No famine "just happens." The famine is covenant discipline for Israel's idolatry (cf. Deut 28:23–24; Lev 26:23–26). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-8-commentary)
- The seven-year duration is significant: seven signals a divinely determined, complete period. The Pulpit Commentary notes that seven years was the duration of Joseph's famine in Egypt and that some meteorologists see "seven years" as a cyclic weather period. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik notes the famine was double the length of Elijah's famine (cf. James 5:17) — a just increase in severity since Israel remained stubborn despite Elisha's ministry. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- **Chronology question (Precept Austin, citing MacArthur):** Three views exist: (1) the encounter took place late in Jehoram's reign (problem: Gehazi would be leprous, and the king already knew Elisha's works); (2) it occurred early in Jehu's reign (same Gehazi problem); (3) best explanation — the record is out of chronological sequence, occurring earlier in Jehoram's reign before 2 Kings 5:1–7:20, thematically tied to the famine of 6:24–7:20. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-8-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — *"So the woman had proceeded to do as the man of God had instructed…"*

- The Shunammite's immediate obedience is commended: "It is a satisfaction to find that there was yet faith in Israel." Even as a woman of substance (2 Kings 4:8), she obeyed without hesitation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Philistia was a grain-producing region less vulnerable to drought because of Mediterranean vapors and dew. Her choice may also have been influenced by proximity and productivity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- God's providence embraced her whole household, not just her. "His care is never half-measured; when He cares for His people, He cares fully, faithfully, and comprehensively." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-8-commentary)

---

### v. 3 — *"At the end of seven years… she went to the king to appeal for her house and her land."*

- During her absence, a grasping neighbor had seized her unoccupied house and uncultivated estate. Widows were especially vulnerable to such land-grabbing (cf. Isa 10:2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik observes that by leaving Israel, the woman forfeited her claim to ancestral lands. Her appeal aimed to ensure she would not be a "loser for listening to God's prophet." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable offers two views of the legal situation: (a) she had sold her property before leaving and now wished to redeem it under Mosaic Law (Lev 25:23–28); (b) she had left it, the crown took it over, and she was reclaiming it as the legal owner. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 4 — *"Now the king had been speaking to Gehazi…"*

- The presence of Gehazi at court suggests these events occurred before his leprosy (2 Kings 5:20–27), since a king would not converse familiarly with a leper. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html) Guzik also notes this, adding that some (e.g., Clarke) suggest the conversation could have happened after Gehazi became leprous if the king kept his distance, but the narrative is best placed earlier. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- The king's motive may have been mere curiosity, but it was still significant testimony: the king of Israel knew God was with Elisha's actions. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- The Pulpit Commentary remarks that it was natural for Jehoram, having witnessed so many of Elisha's public miracles, to want to hear about his private ones from a reliable eyewitness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 5 — *"Just then the woman whose son Elisha had revived came to appeal…"*

- The timing was no coincidence. "Divine providence so ordered matters that, just when the king's interest in the woman was most warm, she should appear before him to urge her claim." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Gehazi was recounting the very miracle of raising the dead — the greatest of Elisha's miracles — at the exact moment the woman and her son appeared. This "perfect, God-ordained timing" moved the king. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Gehazi identifies both the woman and her son (now a boy of ten or eleven) as the actual objects of Elisha's miracle. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 6 — *"Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field…"*

- The king appointed a "certain officer" (literally, a eunuch or chamberlain) to enforce the restoration. Not only was her house and land returned, but she also received "the mesne profits" — the full value of all the land had produced beyond cultivation costs during her seven-year absence. The Pulpit Commentary notes that English law follows the same principle in cases of unlawful possession. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik cites Dilday: "This act was in striking contrast to the notorious land-grabbing of Jehoram's father, Ahab." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable: "God blessed the woman for her obedience … He not only restored her house and land but also the produce of her land… Thus the Israelites saw that Yahweh is the lord of time who brings blessing on the faithful." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 7 — *"Then Elisha came to Damascus while Ben-hadad king of Aram was sick…"*

- Elisha's reason for going to Damascus is not stated. Rashi speculated it was to fetch back Gehazi; Keil thought he went to anoint Hazael per Elijah's charge (1 Kings 19:15); Ewald believed Elisha retreated to Damascus due to strained relations with Jehoram. All rest on conjecture; a divine impulse likely led him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/8.htm — via search excerpt)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes it was a bold step given the Syrian king's earlier efforts to capture Elisha (2 Kings 6:13–19). Yet the Syrians now gave him the respectful title "the man of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik: "The leaders of Syria once tried to capture or kill Elisha. Since God miraculously delivered the prophet so many times, he was now respected and welcomed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 8 — *"Take a gift in your hand, go to meet the man of God…"*

- Ben-hadad's inquiry — "Shall I recover from this disease?" — shows that Elisha's miracles had convinced the Syrians that Jehovah was a great God and Elisha a true prophet. The Pulpit Commentary remarks that "it was by these and similar weakenings of established errors that the world was gradually educated, and the way prepared for the introduction of Christianity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Hazael is described by Josephus as "the most faithful of the king's domestics." Bringing a present to a prophet was customary both among Israelites and heathens (cf. 1 Sam 9:7; 1 Kings 14:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Constable notes: "The Gentile King of Aram had more interest in inquiring of Yahweh than Jehoram's predecessor did (cf. 2 Kings 1:2)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 9 — *"…a gift of forty camel loads of every good thing from Damascus."*

- The present was ostentatious: gold, silver, costly raiment, the luscious wine of Helbon, white wool of Antilibanus, Damascus blades, and goods from Tyre, Egypt, Nineveh, and Babylon. Forty camels paraded the gift — Oriental practice often used many bearers for what one person could carry. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik, citing Poole, suggests Elisha probably did not accept the gift, based on his refusal of Naaman's gift (2 Kings 5) for the same reasons. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Ben-hadad calls himself Elisha's "son," a gesture of deference and respect. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 10 — *"Go and tell him, 'You will surely recover.' But the LORD has shown me that in fact he will die."*

- A textual issue exists: the received Hebrew text (Kethib) has *lo* ("not"), but the margin (Qere) and all ancient versions read *lo* ("to him"). The correct reading is "Go, say to him, 'You shall surely live'" — the strong affirmative. The king *would* recover from his illness, but he would still die — by Hazael's hand, not by disease. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik: "Elisha rightly said that the king would certainly recover from his illness, and he did. However, he also saw that the same servant he spoke with … would engineer an assassination." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable: "Ben-Hadad would have recovered (v. 10) if Hazael had not murdered him (v. 15)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary: "If Hazael had reported the whole answer to Benhadad, he would have told no lie, and thus Elisha is not responsible for his lie." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 11 — *"Elisha fixed his gaze steadily on him until Hazael became uncomfortable. Then the man of God began to weep."*

- Elisha's stare was a long, meaning look by which he penetrated Hazael's soul. The Pulpit Commentary speculates that "the ambitious courtier had already formed a murderous design against his master, and understood by the peculiar gaze … that his design was penetrated." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik, quoting Morgan: "The prophet gazed long and fixedly into the eyes of Hazael. It would seem that he saw far more in the soul of the man than any other had seen, perhaps more than the man himself was conscious of." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable: Elisha "perhaps hoping to embarrass him out of doing the deed." Hazael became ashamed because he felt Elisha could read his mind. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Elisha's weeping reflects the prophet's burden: seeing what would befall Israel through Hazael but being powerless to prevent it. Guzik quotes Meyer: "The nearer we live to God, the more we deserve to be known as men and women of God, the more will our tears flow for the slain of the daughters of our people." And Morgan: "His tears … were the outcome of his deep love for his people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 12 — *"Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites…"*

- The horrors listed — burning fortresses, killing young men, dashing children, ripping open pregnant women — were customary horrors of ancient Near Eastern warfare, not unique to Hazael. They are attested in Psalms 137:9; 2 Kings 15:16; Isaiah 13:16, 18; Hosea 10:14; Nahum 3:10; Amos 1:13. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Hazael would be God's instrument of judgment on Israel (cf. 1 Kings 19:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- These wars of Hazael against Israel are recorded in 2 Kings 10:32–33; 13:3–7; and Amos 1:3–4. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 13 — *"But how could your servant, a mere dog, do such a monstrous thing?"*

- The phrase "a dog" is a term of extreme contempt in the ancient Near East (cf. 1 Sam 24:14; 2 Sam 16:9). Hazael is not accusing Elisha of calling him a dog; rather, he calls *himself* a dog, meaning: "How could someone in my poor and humble position do so great a thing?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Constable adds that Hazael came from lowly stock: "On one Assyrian record Shalmaneser referred to him as 'the son of a nobody.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- **Spurgeon's insight (via Guzik):** "Our ignorance of the depravity of our own hearts is a startling fact. Hazael did not believe that he was bad enough to do any of the things here anticipated… I appeal to you, Christian men and women, if anyone had told you that you would have loved your Savior so little as you have done… would you have believed it!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Elisha's reply — "The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram" — explains how Hazael would be in a position to do these things. Like Saul, David, and Solomon, Hazael learned he would be king by special revelation. But unlike David, Hazael did not wait for God to place him on the throne. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik addresses whether Elisha set a self-fulfilling prophecy in motion: Elisha did not tell Hazael *how* the king would die or *how* he would become king. He spoke against his own compassionate and patriotic interests, suggesting he did so at God's prompting. Perhaps he hoped the prophecy would touch Hazael's heart and turn him from evil. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 14 — *"He told me that you would surely recover."*

- Hazael gave only half the answer, suppressing the other half. "The suppressio veri is a suggestio falsi; and the suppression was Hazael's act, not Elisha's." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik, citing Poole: "He represents the prophet's answer by halves, that by his master's security he might have the fitter opportunity to execute his treasonable design." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 15 — *"Hazael took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king's face."*

- The *macber* was a coarse cloth or mat, probably used as a pillow between the head-rest and the head. Dipping it in water filled the interstices through which air might pass, hastening suffocation. The Pulpit Commentary notes a similar death recorded in Persian history. Some commentators (Luther, Schultz, Geddes) thought Ben-hadad accidentally suffocated himself, but this is unlikely — Hazael is the natural subject of all the verbs. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)
- Constable: Hazael "did so in a manner that made it look as though the king had died of natural causes." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik, citing Spurgeon on predestination and free agency: "The predestination of God does not destroy the free agency of man, or lighten the responsibility of the sinner… in sinning, man is free — free in the widest sense of the term, never being compelled to do any evil deed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- **NET Bible note:** The NET translates "took a piece of cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over Ben Hadad's face until he died." The translation note on the NET indicates the murder was Hazael's act. (https://netbible.org/bible/2+Kings+8)
- An ancient Assyrian inscription (the Berlin inscription) says, "Hazael the son of nobody, seized the throne," confirming he was a usurper with no dynastic line. (Quoted by Guzik from Dilday) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Hazael ruled 841–801 B.C. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 16 — *"In the fifth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab over Israel, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat succeeded his father as king of Judah."*

- The writer picks up the story of the kings of Judah from 1 Kings 22:50, where Jehoshaphat's reign ended. This King Jehoram of Judah is not to be confused with the King Jehoram (Joram) of Israel from 2 Kings 3. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable explains the chronology: Jehoshaphat appointed Jehoram coregent in 853 B.C. (when Jehoshaphat joined Ahab at Ramoth-gilead). Jehoram ruled with his father five years, then alone from 848–841 B.C. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions lack the phrase "Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah," suggesting it may be a gloss that crept into the text. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 17 — *"Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years."*

- The Chronicler records that Jehoram made all Judah to sin according to the religion of the Canaanites (2 Chron 21:11). Obadiah may have prophesied during his reign. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 18 — *"And Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel… For he married a daughter of Ahab."*

- This was a spiritual calamity. The marriage to Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, may have made political sense but brought Judah down spiritually. "Perhaps some people thought that the marriage between the royal families … would lift up the kingdom of Israel spiritually. It didn't work that way. Instead, it brought the kingdom of Judah down spiritually." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Guzik (in his devotional): "2 Kings 8:18 tells us part of the reason so much wickedness came from King Jehoram: *for the daughter of Ahab was his wife*. The evil influence of the house of Ahab was strong in Jehoram's life." (https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/sake-of-another/)
- Constable: "Rather than following the godly example of his father, Jehoram chose to pursue idolatry and infidelity to Yahweh like his wife Athaliah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik cites Josephus (via Dilday): Jehoram murdered his many brothers and other leaders "at the prompting of Athaliah" to consolidate his throne (cf. 2 Chron 21:4–6). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 19 — *"Yet for the sake of His servant David, the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah…"*

- The implication is that Jehoram's evil was great enough to justify destruction, but God withheld judgment out of faithfulness to His covenant with David (2 Sam 7:12–15). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable: "If it had not been for His promise to David … God would have cut off Jehoram's line for his wickedness." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- The "lamp" (*nir*) was a symbol of life, testimony, and the Davidic covenant (cf. Ps 132:17; 2 Chron 21:7). (Quoted by Guzik from Wiseman) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 20 — *"In the days of Jehoram, Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah…"*

- Edom had been under Judah's control during Jehoshaphat's reign (2 Chron 20:1–29; 1 Kings 22:47). Its revolt evidences the weakness of Jehoram. "He thought that the marriage alliance with Ahab … would make Judah stronger, but this act of disobedience only made them weaker." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Constable: "Instead [of destroying Judah], he disciplined him and Judah by allowing Edom and Libnah to revolt against Judah successfully." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 21 — *"So Jehoram crossed over to Zair with all his chariots…"*

- Zair is another name for Seir or Edom. Jehoram was surrounded at night; he broke out, but his troops fled to their tents — a military failure. "Chariots did not save Jehoram from defeat." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### v. 22 — *"So to this day Edom has been in rebellion… Likewise, Libnah rebelled at the same time."*

- Libnah was a town near the border between Judah and Philistia, likely revolting when the Philistines invaded Judah (2 Chron 21:16–17). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)

---

### vv. 23–24 — *"As for the rest of the acts of Jehoram… And Jehoram rested with his fathers…"*

- The Chronicler adds that Elijah wrote Jehoram a letter condemning his sins and predicting judgment (2 Chron 21:12–15). At age 40, Jehoram was struck with a fatal intestinal disease and died in terrible pain (2 Chron 21:19). He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the honored tombs of his ancestors (2 Chron 21:20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Guzik quotes Knapp: "He is one of the most unlovely of all the kings of Judah. 'Exalted by Jehovah,' he was for his wickedness thrust down to a dishonoured grave." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 25 — *"In the twelfth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab over Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah."*

- Constable details the chronology: there were two King Ahaziahs and two King Jehorams — one of each in each kingdom. Ahaziah of Israel reigned 853–852 B.C.; Ahaziah of Judah reigned in 841 B.C. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik cites Patterson and Austel: "Ahaziah succeeded his father, Jehoram, in the critical year 841 B.C. He was not to survive the momentous waves of the political events that were to inundate the ancient Near East in that year." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 26 — *"Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king… His mother's name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri king of Israel."*

- There is a well-known numerical discrepancy: 2 Chronicles 22:2 says Ahaziah was 42 years old when he began to reign, which would make him older than his own father (who died at 40). Guzik, quoting Clarke, regards the 42 in Chronicles as a scribal error and says the correct reading is 22, as here. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 27 — *"And Ahaziah walked in the ways of the house of Ahab… for he was a son-in-law of the house of Ahab."*

- Ahaziah continued the policies of his great-grandfather Omri, his grandfather Ahab, and his uncle Joram. The NET Bible renders this as "for he was related to Ahab's family," highlighting the marriage alliance that pulled Judah into spiritual decline. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html; https://netbible.org/bible/2+Kings+8)

---

### v. 28 — *"Then Ahaziah went with Joram son of Ahab to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and the Arameans wounded Joram."*

- This battle took place about 12 years after the one in which Ahab and Jehoshaphat fought at Ramoth-gilead and Ahab died (1 Kings 22:3, 29). Ahaziah's close association with the house of Ahab developed into a war alliance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

### v. 29 — *"So King Joram returned to Jezreel… Then Ahaziah … went down to Jezreel to visit Joram…"*

- Jezreel was Joram's winter capital. Ahaziah's visit to his wounded uncle sets the stage for the events of 2 Kings 9, where both kings will meet their end at the hands of Jehu. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Guzik: "His connection with his mother's family … was so strong and sympathetic that he paid a visit to the injured and sick king of Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

## Section 2: Points of Difference among Protestant Traditions

Given the available sources, denominational distinctives are less pronounced on this narrative chapter than on doctrinal passages. However, several emphases emerge:

**Reformed / Sovereign Grace Emphasis (Spurgeon, via Guzik):**
- On v. 13: Hazael's response reveals a universal blindness to the depravity of the human heart. Spurgeon used this to urge self-examination among believers: "if any prophet had told you, in the hour of your conversion, that you would have served him so feebly as you have done, would you have believed it!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- On v. 15: Spurgeon stressed that predestination does not destroy free agency in sin: "in sinning, man is free — free in the widest sense of the term, never being compelled to do any evil deed, but being left to follow the turbulent passions of his own corrupt heart." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

**Evangelical / Dispensational (Constable, MacArthur via Precept Austin):**
- Emphasis on God's control of timing and history: "Yahweh is the lord of time who brings blessing on the faithful." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- The famine is treated as covenant discipline per Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26 — "this was one of the curses" (Utley, via Precept Austin). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-8-commentary)
- MacArthur's three-position chronology (via Precept Austin) reflects a careful evangelical approach to harmonizing apparent discrepancies. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-8-commentary)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):**
- Emphasis on the prophetic calling as both gift and burden: Elisha's tears show the emotional weight of prophetic insight. The prophet's "deep love for his people" is underscored. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)
- Guzik highlights divine "perfect, God-ordained timing" in the Shunammite's appearance before the king. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-8/)

---

## Section 3: Other Views

**Modern Scholarship / NET Bible:**
- The NET Bible translates v. 10 as "Go and tell him, 'You will surely recover,' but the Lord has revealed to me that he will surely die" — resolving the textual issue by adopting the Qere reading (*lo*, "to him") over the Kethib (*lo*, "not"). (https://netbible.org/bible/2+Kings+8)
- The NET notes (summarized in Constable) treat the chronology as complex and overlapping, noting the coregency periods that explain apparent discrepancies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
- Constable references Assyrian records confirming Hazael as "son of a nobody" and the Black Obelisk inscription confirming Hazael as successor to Ben-Hadad II. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-8.html)
